newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Hunger stalks Kabul as Islamic festival arrives.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hunger stalks Kabul as Islamic festival arrives.

text.p: Snow whirls down on war-shattered Kabul and Mohammad Yasin is in deep thought about what to cook for his guests on next week's Moslem festival of Eid al-Fitr.
He also needs to buy new clothes for his four children, but he may not manage it.
On a muddy sidewalk in one of Kabul's markets, Yasin, a Kabul University graduate, sells vegetables to make a living, a tough challenge in the destroyed capital after 17 years of civil war.

He has been displaced three times during factional fighting for the control of Kabul after the collapse of the communist government in early 1992, and his wife was killed by an artillery shell that fell on a wedding ceremony.
Yasin started washing cars for a living, but that did not last for long, he says. He was beaten by a guerrilla commander for scratching his car and forced to pay a compensation equivalent to $20.
With his new job as a greengrocer, he earns about $30 a month, which is a fortune compared to the very low wages of most high-ranking civil servants.

"I thank God that I am not holding out my hand to beg and have assets to run a small business," he told Reuters. "I wonder how those government employees live who are paid the equivalent of $5 a month."
Ismael Omar, a World Food Programme employee, said he met a well-known former government minister one day who asked for food because it was not proper for him to ask for money in the bazaar.
"I could not refuse...so I took him to a warehouse and asked him to help himself," Omar said.
HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS NEEDY
Kabul has hundreds of thousands of needy people who, like the ex-minister, are spending days at the gates of foreign aid agencies asking for help, and most of them are not lucky enough to get it.

Almost 100,000 more have recently arrived in Kabul after fleeing homes north of the capital because of fighting there between the Taleban Islamic movement, which rules Kabul, and an alliance of forces of ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani and Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
"Some people in Kabul go to bed with empty stomachs during this cold winter", a foreign aid worker said.
People like Yasin regard themselves as the middle class of this war-ravaged city, most of whose population faces financial and psychological problems owing to years of a difficult life.
Many have taken to begging because they have no job while food prices are rising.
FOREIGN AID LACKING
Kabulis are in a bad state and aid given by foreign agencies is insufficient, an Afghan Red Crescent Society official said while asking for urgent international aid for them.

"My brother was saying to me that if France announces that all Afghans can settle there should they walk all the way from Afghanistan to there, I believe every one will leave this wretched land," a local journalist said.

Yasin has lost or sold almost all his household goods in the past four years of factional fighting and was forced to move to a safe area from a war zone where armed groups used to break into his house to help themselves to whatever they wanted.
His most nutritious dish is beans and carrots, which he can afford, while meat is a dream.
He said he was now trying to work out how to produce a meal for guests who would come to congratulate him on the Eid, a feast day for Moslems. His four children also need new clothes.
The festival could fall on Sunday or Monday, depending on the sighting of the moon.
Yasin typifies those who at least can live off their own income and do not have to rely on others. And it does not matter to him if he cannot provide the essentials for Eid.

"When I see the living standard of my neighbours and relatives, I think I am the richest of all of them," he said. "At least, if buying meat is out of my reach, beans and potatoes are affordable," he says brushing snow from his neck.
He said was saddened every time he recalled the story told by a friend of a neighbour who had to sell his 10-year-old son because of poverty.

"His second son, a 15 years old, was killed by a mine when he was collecting twigs and dead leaves in a destroyed part of Kabul, fearing that if he did not earn a living he would also be given to somebody for money."
